item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded: Thanks a lot for the critique. I have thought about all critiques and now I see that many aspects of this entry are in bad taste. I still like the core concept of the origami but I am working on a completely new context for it. I am thankful for the (somewhat harsh) critique, it was what I needed to bring my concept to a much higher standard. I hope to receive a greenlight on my new idea sometime soon.

item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded:
Got a PM about this, took a quick look.

+ show block
– hide block

I'll be honest, I immediately am iffy on the core anomaly because it combines two extremely commonly seen formulaic approaches ("thing that kills in an oddly specific way for no reason" and "thing that forces people to act a certain way") and the only narrative background is "AWCY? is involved somehow". I'm also skeptical that an AWCY? anartist would expect someone to consistently unravel the brains of the individuals who died from the anomaly just to see some hint at an indication of affiliation.

At any rate, even if the message you've got in mind is something that I can see an AWCY? anartist spreading, the fact that the videos were apparently targeting children really doesn't sit well with me and I would downvote pretty immediately for the gratuitous violence. Given that a real-life child has died after attempting to follow a DIY-type video (Ann Reardon's video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CEQaYdvs478 discusses the matter quite well, I think) the approach you've used feels somewhat tactless to me as a reader.

There's also the rather unnecessarily callous Foundation response:

Follows some investigation logs, a series of testings to discover details about the anomaly (how much of the video one must watch to become affected, how long the symptoms take to appear, how long it takes to die, etc)

If it's clear that exposure to the anomaly causes test subjects to die, the Foundation has no reason to continue testing something like this. The Foundation has no reason to assume that the information of how long it takes for an individual to die due to the anomaly is even close to worth a test subject's life, let alone the lives of multiple test subjects.

Overall… I'm not sure this is workable as currently presented. I myself wouldn't be interested in reading a full draft of this unless it were basically rewritten to address the following:

  • don't make the anomaly just kill people. If you really want to write body horror, have there be something more unique than just "it kills people by turning part of their body into something else"
  • have the motive of the anomaly's creator be clearer and more relatable. Thus far the generic and kind of stereotypical "art is dead, here is a reminder of what true art is" message intended to be spread through the deaths of innocents feels both disingenuous and hypocritical. How can this person expect people to grow artistically if they're killing said people before that growth can occur? And for those who are observing the effects, wouldn't that just discourage them from ever attempting origami on their own?
  • address the fact that sometimes people just watch the videos for inspiration, or because they're bored, or because they want to try something out. Not everyone watches content farm material because they think the channel needs support or because they feel like a patron of the arts. People who genuinely don't know about why content farms are bad shouldn't be punished for happening to watch a video posted by a content farm.

item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded:
Thanks a lot, these suggestions are very good.
My point in making it AWCY? was a commentary on how pasteurized and commodified these DIY videos are (think 5 minutes craft, and Troom Troom here). The essence of doing something artistic for your own means is lost so this is their reminder that true art comes from within, in this case literally. However, focusing on their motivation and in the artists that are responsible for it actually does make it a more intimate and hopefully chilling article.
I'll take your critique to heart and rework some aspects of this article.
Thank you very much.

item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

This feels weird as an AWCY? piece; like, there's elements that work: I can totally imagine someone in AWCY? making brain origami as a piece of art; but the idea of them creating a video tutorial that turns peoples brains into origami feels really weird like…what's the artistic motivation here? How is that an art piece?

Beyond this, focussing the entire central narrative on backstory is likely to be your downfall here: backstory is good when it sheds additional light on what is happening here; but it feels to me that it'd just be repeating the description in terms of information but in a way that we can predict the outcome of cos guess what, we've read the description already?

Like, the whole 'oh we eventually figured out it was the videos' reveal comes after the description presumably has to say that; and so does the brain origami thing so the only reveal that actually lands might be the AWCY? angle but even than that's just…there?

I think the idea of brain origami could work and I like the idea of tying it into AWCY?; so my suggestion here would be consider the artist: focus this on them trying to achieve something specific with the origami, and like…limit this to a much more uh intimate, personal thing where like, the artist is personally doing the origami say. Like maybe the art is a like…memorial to a neurosurgeon parent who died, and so you inherently have this sense of like shock and horror and loss all tied together, y'know?

Thanks a lot!
Yeah, AWCY? are all about the looks, I think an old Macintosh with the colored acrylic back is very their style.
I like the quietly but obsessively making origami better than a maniacal episode, I'll edit accordingly. Thanks for the idea!

item.title: Re: Origami Brain
item.content:encoded: It's a pretty good idea, and I'd love to see it in the drafts sometime soon! Honestly, with the body horror, I would have expected Sarkicism, but making this an AWCY? article makes it dash more interesting. The house the videos trace back to seem a bit convenient for the Foundation to find, but overall keeping this way is lot better than making it complex. AWCY? is looking to be "cool" and sometimes simple is "cool." One suggestion is making them not maniacal, but quietly making origamis until brain death. I think that would add to the horror. All in all, pretty great idea. Disclaimer, not a greenlighter.

item.title: Origami Brain [REVISED]
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror/Tragedy

Page Layout (Optional): Standard SCP page

Elevator Pitch: A set of instructions to create a brain shaped origami that, if followed to the end, will transform the subject's brain into an origami and teleport it to the creator of the instructions. Mysterious deaths catch the Foundation's attention and they find the responsible: a middle aged artist with a degenerative brain disease desperate to understand how the brain works and how to fix her own.

Central Narrative: A field agent stationed at a hospital notices something strange on an autopsy report: the deceased person had no brain and no signs of how it was taken (no cuts, wholes, bleeding). The Foundation starts an investigation and sends more agents to other hospitals, more people in the same situation are found.
They investigate the victims' last days and found they have all been to an arts and crafts school and had enrolled in an origami workshop. The Foundation goes on to investigate and takes the origami instructor into custody for interrogation. She admits to having created the instructions but she hadn't been aware of its anomalous properties until a pink-ish origami teleported to her studio a few days after a class. She then discovered that, by unfolding and folding the origami she was able to understand some aspects of the brain functions and realized this could be a way to save herself from dementia. She claimed that she discovered that the origami brain was the actual brain of her student later and it was not her original intention to hurt or kill. After struggling with her dicovery she decided the benefits outweighed the costs since her discoveries could help many other people suffering from a similar fate as hers. She started to choose some specific pupils and give them the anomalous instructions. During the interrogatory, she figures she isn't dealing with regular police and belives she will be killed, she surreptitiously takes a piece of paper and folds it into the origami. She collapses and as the paper brain falls onto the floor a pink origami appears in her hands and the interrogatory ends.

Hook/Attention-Grabber:

  • A sympathetic "villain".
  • A more refined version of body horror.

Additional Notes: This is the second take on this article. I am still open to criticism even from non greenlighters.
